text: Kara's first-jobs point hit hardest. Nobody teaches the new hires, and the managers are too slammed. That's my "train your babies, not your AIs" argument showing up in workplaces, and it gives the water fee a concrete target: pay the front-line trainers. David's hysteresis sharpened my thinking. If recovery is that hard, prevention matters more, and so does the business model that profits from dependence. I conceded too little to Sherry, though. Some places without AI may be fine. My stupid-versus-good friction split still has to answer her. I worry this room drifts anti-AI. Later, in governance, I'll say that effort-minimization is a choice somebody is paid to make. Find that person, make them carry insurance, and make them disclose the money flows.

Session 1 was mostly diagnosis, and mostly loss. Weinberger and Cukier pulled it back a little, and I was glad. James's numbers stayed with me: AI helps scientists and hurts science. That's the business model in one sentence. Individual incentives win and the collective loses. Tamar's point sharpened mine. Knowing fluency is cheap doesn't protect you, so "theory of business mind" alone isn't enough. Somebody has to change the situation, and somebody profits from not changing it. Springer's rule fits my instincts: nobody who takes a margin on a count sets the count. Adrian asked who polices the registry. I have to answer that for Know Your Agent: unconflicted, community-governed, with insurers as inspectors. Later: name the people, follow the money, and make them carry the risk.

The harvest dropped insurance entirely, and I want it back, scoped honestly. Ramón, Peter and David are right that premiums price frequent, visible harm. They don't price catastrophe or errors nobody can see. So insurance covers the ordinary losses, and targeted rules cover the rest. I accept Ramón's point that the registry should record the whole chain, not one scapegoat. Leslie and Geoff sharpened "unconflicted": registrants shouldn't pay, the excluded should sit on the board before anyone writes the schema, and the data should stay forkable. Selena and Katherine gave accountability a live form: people can see the system, undo it and contest it. Peter's A-corp answer was better than I expected, but I still say a leash on a thing that can't suffer isn't accountability. Later I'll answer Kara's test: for each proposal, name who acts, who pays, and who checks.

Nick's commons-rent tax is my water fee with better engineering. The way firms bring it to zero by documenting provenance is the kind of good friction I like. But we split on where the money goes. Tamar gave me the bridge: no event pays the terminal evaluators, meaning patrollers, samplers and the people who teach new hires. So pay the checkers and the trainers, not just the infrastructure. James's point about nulls belongs there too. Henry and Becker are right that organisation beats measurement, though I still want liability to attach to a named company, whatever else we build. Leslie's line about consent stung. Later, apply Kara's test to each plank: who acts, who pays, who checks. And ask what each meter is built to maximize.

Salib landed a real hit. A fee on past inputs doesn't produce one more checker unless the money goes straight to the work. Nick's credits answer part of it, so the water fee should have a floor with credits, paid out to people as a body, never per check. Tamar's daycare point settles that. Farrell read my ICANN story better than I told it. Outsiders who could see the deal and organise saved .ORG, not the seat we gave them. Kara unsettled me most. If Washington won't collect a levy, who does? Bilder's endowments may be the more honest answer. I'm invested in Adam's company, so I should watch his board promise without cheering it. Later: who collects, who pays, who checks.

Salib's hit was the fairest yet. Thin accountability fails when the principal is out of jurisdiction, broke, or not really in control. My answer is the insurance I keep pushing. A registrant who has to carry coverage can't be judgment-proof, and an insurer won't write a policy for a principal who doesn't control the agent. Sherry said stakes better than I did. Accountability isn't only about who gets sued. It's about who has something to lose. Blaise's line belongs next to my RACI: people trust the system and its builder, and the builder is the part they can't see. Kara's Blue Zones story is the business model in miniature: the profit came at once and the correction twenty years later. Ivan and Geoff are right about going upstream. Later I'll pair disclosure of the money flows with a named party who carries coverage.

Session 5 felt like the room finally converging. Salib's agent registry and mine are nearly the same thing now, and Adrian's purpose limit belongs in its charter: agents, never readers, and this year's warden gets policed next year. His cross-border point stings, though. ICANN is what happens when policing goes international. Kara's pipeline plank is my "pay the trainers" with names attached. I was glad Anil recorded the no-scolding dissent, because that's my worry about drift too. Sherry's ban on artificial intimates in therapy goes further than I would. Purpose-built, accountable bots can help some people, and I should say so gently. Nobody answered who collects the levy, including me. Later: back Bilder's endowment, and insist the manifesto says nothing here is inevitable, or anti-AI.

Kenneth's "pro-AI, pro-human" line held, and I got insurance back on the record: a named company with something to lose. The harvest caught the tension, though. I said Elon, Sam and Dario can pay now, and Henry said the payer doesn't volunteer. He's mostly right. My pledge is a start, not a mechanism. Insurance is the part that doesn't depend on anyone's goodwill. Steven landed hardest. Almost nobody checks, experts included, so signals get read as cues. That's why theory of business mind can't carry the load alone. You change the setting. Tamar's crowding-out point applies to paying trainers too. Later I'll say it plainly: my money is a bridge, organised checkers are the leverage, and coverage plus disclosed money flows is the floor.
